root.subtitle: Membrane structure, selective routes and protein topology
root.examSkill: Distinguish membrane embedding from spanning; link the stated molecule and transport route to structure.

voiceover.text: The Fluid Mosaic Membrane. Year eleven Biology. Cells as the basis of life.

hook.body: Oxygen can diffuse through the bilayer. Na⁺ normally crosses by a suitable transport protein.
hook.callout: Structure and molecular properties explain selective permeability.
hook.caption: Different molecular properties require different routes.

voiceover.text: Oxygen and sodium ions interact differently with a membrane. Small non-polar oxygen molecules can diffuse through the lipid bilayer. A sodium ion has an extremely low permeability through that hydrophobic core and normally crosses by a suitable transport protein. The membrane does not make a conscious choice. Molecular properties and available pathways determine movement.

bullets.text: Hydrophilic heads face aqueous fluid on both sides.
Hydrophobic tails form the inner core.
O₂ crosses readily; ions have very low lipid-bilayer permeability.

concept-bilayer.callout: Permeability is a property and a rate, not a conscious decision.
concept-bilayer.caption: Hydrophilic heads out, hydrophobic tails in; routes differ by substance.

voiceover.text: In this model, phospholipids have hydrophilic heads facing water and hydrophobic tails facing inward. The resulting core presents a barrier to ions and many polar molecules. Small non-polar molecules such as oxygen cross comparatively readily. This is selective permeability, rather than an absolute all-or-nothing wall. Lipids move laterally within their own layer.

concept-proteins.body: Integral means embedded. Transmembrane specifically means spanning the bilayer.

bullets.text: Transmembrane proteins are a subset of integral proteins.
Some integral proteins do not cross the whole bilayer.
Channels provide selective aqueous paths; carriers operate differently.
Peripheral proteins associate with the surface; glycoproteins carry carbohydrates.

concept-proteins.callout: A spanning example does not define every integral protein.
concept-proteins.caption: Integral proteins need not span; transmembrane proteins do span.

voiceover.text: Integral proteins are embedded in the bilayer. Transmembrane proteins are the subset that span it from one side to the other. Some integral proteins enter and leave the same side without spanning the whole membrane. The large spanning protein drawn here is a transmembrane example. Channels provide selective aqueous paths. Peripheral proteins associate with a membrane surface, often through other proteins. Glycoproteins carry carbohydrate chains involved in recognition and signalling.

concept-cholesterol.body: In animal-cell membranes, cholesterol modifies lipid packing and fluidity.

bullets.text: Effects depend on temperature and lipid composition.
Cholesterol can restrain movement in warmer conditions.
It can hinder close packing in colder conditions.

concept-cholesterol.callout: State the model and conditions before predicting.
concept-cholesterol.caption: Cholesterol modulates membrane properties; effects are context dependent.

voiceover.text: Cholesterol is an important component of animal-cell membranes. It changes lipid packing and buffers fluidity: it can restrain lipid movement at higher temperatures and hinder tight packing at lower temperatures. Its effect depends on membrane composition and conditions. This is a simplified model, not a guarantee that every membrane has a fixed fluidity or that removing cholesterol always has one exact outcome.

bullets.text: Bilayer: two lipid layers, hydrophobic regions inward.
Integral protein: embedded in the membrane.
Transmembrane protein: an integral protein spanning the membrane.
Monotopic integral protein: embedded from one side, not spanning both.
Peripheral: surface-associated. Glycoprotein: carbohydrate-bearing protein.

definition.callout: Glycoprotein and transmembrane can describe the same protein.
definition.caption: Embedded, spanning, surface-associated and carbohydrate-bearing are distinct properties.

voiceover.text: Keep the categories separate. A bilayer is two lipid layers with hydrophobic regions inward. An integral protein is embedded in that membrane. A transmembrane protein spans the membrane, while a monotopic integral protein associates with one leaflet without spanning both. A peripheral protein is surface-associated. A glycoprotein bears carbohydrate groups. These labels describe different structural features and are not mutually exclusive categories.

worked-example.question: Explain why O₂ can diffuse through the lipid bilayer, whereas passive Na⁺ movement through a suitable open channel depends on its electrochemical gradient.
steps: O₂ is small and non-polar; it can enter the hydrophobic core.
Na⁺ is charged and has very low permeability through the lipid core.
An open selective channel provides an aqueous route.
Net passive ion movement follows the electrochemical gradient.
A channel is one route; other transport proteins can move sodium.
worked-example.coachNote: Explain the stated route without claiming every protein works as a channel.
worked-example.caption: O₂: bilayer diffusion. Na⁺: a selective channel and electrochemical driving force.

voiceover.text: Explain the route from structure. Oxygen is small and non-polar, so it can dissolve in and diffuse through the bilayer. Sodium is charged, so the hydrophobic core is a major barrier. A suitable sodium channel provides an aqueous route, and passive net movement depends on the electrochemical gradient. Channels are not the only sodium transport proteins: pumps and coupled carriers also exist. The question specifies a passive channel route.

misconception.heading: Two overgeneralisations
misconception.body: Wrong: every integral protein spans the membrane and every protein drifts freely.
misconception.secondary: Integral proteins can be monotopic or transmembrane. Protein motion may be constrained by attachments and membrane organisation.
misconception.callout: Fluid mosaic is a useful model with limits.
misconception.caption: Embedding does not imply spanning; fluidity does not imply unrestricted motion.

voiceover.text: Two distinctions matter. Fluid does not mean every protein moves freely without constraint. Many lipids and proteins move laterally, while some proteins are anchored or confined. Integral also does not mean transmembrane in every case. A protein may be embedded from one side. Use the actual topology, not just the word integral, to decide whether a protein spans the bilayer.

quick-check.question: A protein has a hydrophobic segment embedded in one leaflet. Both ends remain on the cytoplasmic side. Is it integral, transmembrane, or both?
answerSteps: It is integral because it is embedded in the bilayer.
It is not transmembrane because it does not cross to the other side.
quick-check.caption: Classify using the stated topology.

voiceover.text: A protein is embedded in one leaflet and both ends are on the cytoplasmic side. Is it integral, transmembrane, or both? Pause and explain. It is integral because it is embedded. It is not transmembrane because it does not span the bilayer. This is a monotopic topology.

points: The bilayer has an aqueous-facing surface and hydrophobic core.
Permeability differs among substances.
Integral means embedded; transmembrane means spanning.
Channels, carriers and surface-associated proteins have different roles.
Glycoproteins contribute to recognition; cholesterol modulates animal membranes.
summary.finalPrompt: For a protein, identify its topology before assigning a route.
summary.caption: Membrane structure explains selective permeability and protein roles.

voiceover.text: Use structure to explain function. The lipid bilayer presents a hydrophobic barrier with different permeabilities to different substances. Integral proteins are embedded, and only the transmembrane subset spans the bilayer. Channels and carriers provide selective transport routes. Glycoproteins can contribute to recognition, and cholesterol modifies animal-membrane properties. Keep the model's limits in view.

response.promptText: A protein is embedded in one leaflet and both ends are on the cytoplasmic side. Is it integral, transmembrane, or both? Pause and explain.
response.answerText: It is integral because it is embedded. It is not transmembrane because it does not span the bilayer. This is a monotopic topology.
response.status: planning only; actual silence, answer/caption concealment and cues must be rebuilt

root.subtitle: Filtration, reabsorption, secretion and net excretion

voiceover.text: The Nephron. Year eleven Biology. Cells to systems.

hook.heading: Filter broadly, regulate what remains
hook.body: Much of the filtered water returns to blood. Urine reflects several transport processes.
hook.callout: Waste excretion does not mean zero reabsorption.
hook.caption: Adult daily volumes are examples, not fixed values for everyone.

voiceover.text: The kidneys produce a large volume of filtrate, but most filtered water returns to the blood. A healthy adult example might filter about one hundred and eighty litres per day and excrete one or two litres of urine, though values vary. Filtration, reabsorption and secretion work together. Calling urea a waste product does not mean none of it can return from the tubule.

concept-filtration.body: A pressure difference drives filtration across a selective physical barrier.

bullets.text: Water and many small solutes enter Bowman’s capsule.
Cells and most plasma proteins are normally retained.
Useful glucose and waste urea can both enter the filtrate.

concept-filtration.callout: Physical selectivity is not selection by usefulness.
concept-filtration.caption: Glomerular filtrate contains both useful solutes and wastes.

voiceover.text: Pressure across the glomerular filtration barrier moves water and many small dissolved substances into Bowman's capsule. Blood cells and most plasma proteins are normally retained. The barrier is selective by physical properties, not by whether a substance is useful or waste. Glucose and urea both enter filtrate. Filtration alone is therefore not the final composition of urine.

concept-tubule.heading: Direction and net amount matter
concept-tubule.body: Urea can be reabsorbed and recycled while still being excreted overall.

bullets.text: Reabsorption: tubular fluid towards blood.
Secretion: blood towards tubular fluid.
Some urea is reabsorbed and recycled; the remainder contributes to net excretion.

concept-tubule.callout: Track transport directions, then calculate the net result.
concept-tubule.caption: Schematic paths, not measured transport fractions.

voiceover.text: Reabsorption moves substances from the tubule back towards blood. Secretion moves selected substances in the opposite direction. Glucose and amino acids are normally recovered very effectively, and water and ion transport are regulated. Some filtered urea is reabsorbed and recycled in the kidney, contributing to the medullary concentration gradient. Urea can still be excreted overall. The diagram is schematic and its particle counts are not physiological fractions.

bullets.text: Nephron: microscopic functional unit of the kidney.
Filtration: blood to capsule across the glomerular barrier.
Reabsorption: tubular fluid towards blood.
Secretion: blood towards tubular fluid.
Excretion: loss from the body in urine.

definition.callout: Excretion is an output; it is not the same process as filtration.
definition.caption: Distinguish filtration, reabsorption, secretion and excretion.

voiceover.text: Filtration is movement from glomerular blood into the capsule across the filtration barrier. Reabsorption returns material from tubular fluid towards the blood. Secretion adds material from blood to tubular fluid. Excretion is material leaving the body in urine. A nephron is the kidney's microscopic functional unit. These process names describe direction and destination, not whether a molecule has been labelled useful or waste.

concept-design.body: Kidney transport combines net waste removal with water and solute regulation.

bullets.text: Filtration does not separate useful from waste molecules.
During dehydration, ADH generally increases collecting-duct water reabsorption.
With unchanged tubular solute content and no other sources/sinks: excreted = filtered − reabsorbed + secreted.

concept-design.callout: Same interval; unchanged tubular solute content; no other sources or sinks.
concept-design.caption: Hydration and regulated transport determine urine composition.

voiceover.text: The kidney combines waste removal with regulation. Broad filtration is followed by selective transport. During dehydration, increased vasopressin, also called ADH, generally increases collecting-duct water permeability, helping conserve water. Temperature alone does not determine that response. Urea recycling supports the medullary osmotic environment; this does not prevent net urea excretion. For this simplified interval balance, assume the amount of solute stored in the tubule does not change and there are no other sources or sinks, including production or consumption. Excreted amount then equals filtered minus reabsorbed plus secreted. If tubular content changes, that accumulation must also be included.

worked-example.question: In a synthetic interval balance, 100 units of solute are filtered, 60 reabsorbed and 20 secreted. Assume unchanged tubular solute content over the interval and no other sources or sinks, including production or consumption. Calculate net excretion and explain whether reabsorption prevents excretion.
worked-example.coachNote: Use matched amounts for one solute and interval. The stated no-accumulation and no-other-source/sink assumptions are essential.
steps: With unchanged tubular solute content and no other sources or sinks, net excretion = filtered − reabsorbed + secreted.
Net excretion remains positive despite reabsorption.
The data are illustrative, not a stated normal human urea fraction.
worked-example.caption: Under the stated no-accumulation/source/sink assumptions: 100 − 60 + 20 = 60 units.

voiceover.text: Consider illustrative amounts for one interval. One hundred units are filtered, sixty reabsorbed and twenty secreted. Assume the tubular solute content is unchanged over that interval, with no other sources or sinks such as production or consumption. Under these assumptions, net excretion is one hundred minus sixty plus twenty, or sixty units. These are synthetic amounts, not measured human urea physiology. If solute accumulated in the tubule, the simple calculation would need an accumulation term. Reabsorption can coexist with positive net excretion.

misconception.heading: Waste does not mean never reabsorbed
misconception.body: Wrong: filtration removes only waste, and reabsorption leaves all urea behind.
misconception.secondary: Glucose and urea both enter filtrate. Some urea is reabsorbed and recycled, while net urea excretion still removes nitrogenous waste.
misconception.callout: Urea can be reabsorbed and still be excreted overall.
misconception.caption: Do not classify transport solely by usefulness.

voiceover.text: The kidney does not simply filter wastes and then leave all urea behind. Filtration has physical selectivity and includes many useful small solutes. Later transport returns many substances to blood. That includes some urea. Reabsorption is not restricted to molecules called useful, and excretion does not imply that every filtered molecule followed one uninterrupted path into urine.

quick-check.question: A synthetic interval has 80 units filtered, 50 reabsorbed and 10 secreted. Assume unchanged tubular solute content over the interval and no other sources or sinks, including production or consumption. What is net excretion? Does it imply no reabsorption occurred?
quick-check.pausePrompt: Pause: apply the stated no-accumulation and no-other-source/sink model.
answerSteps: With unchanged tubular solute content and no other sources or sinks: 80 − 50 + 10 = 40 units excreted.
No. The data explicitly include 50 units reabsorbed.
Positive net excretion and reabsorption can coexist.
quick-check.caption: Use the interval balance, not a useful-versus-waste rule.

voiceover.text: Eighty units are filtered, fifty reabsorbed and ten secreted in the same interval. Assume unchanged tubular solute content and no other sources or sinks, including production or consumption. Calculate net excretion. Does excretion mean none was reabsorbed? Under the stated no-accumulation and no-other-source-or-sink assumptions, eighty minus fifty plus ten equals forty units excreted. No. Fifty units were reabsorbed. Net excretion and reabsorption can coexist.

points: Filtration has physical selectivity, not selection by usefulness.
Reabsorption returns material towards blood.
Secretion adds material to tubular fluid.
Some urea is reabsorbed and recycled despite net excretion.
With unchanged tubular solute content and no other sources/sinks: excreted = filtered − reabsorbed + secreted.
summary.finalPrompt: Distinguish transport direction from final net output.
summary.caption: Filter, reabsorb, secrete and excrete are distinct processes.

voiceover.text: Glomerular filtration moves water and many small solutes into the capsule while normally retaining cells and most plasma proteins. Reabsorption returns substances towards blood, secretion adds selected substances to tubular fluid, and excretion is the final urine output. Some urea is reabsorbed and recycled even though urea is excreted overall. For a defined interval, use amounts rather than concentrations alone. The simple filtered-minus-reabsorbed-plus-secreted equation assumes unchanged tubular solute content and no other sources or sinks, including production or consumption.

response.promptText: Eighty units are filtered, fifty reabsorbed and ten secreted in the same interval. Assume unchanged tubular solute content and no other sources or sinks, including production or consumption. Calculate net excretion. Does excretion mean none was reabsorbed?
response.answerText: Under the stated no-accumulation and no-other-source-or-sink assumptions, eighty minus fifty plus ten equals forty units excreted. No. Fifty units were reabsorbed. Net excretion and reabsorption can coexist.

root.subtitle: Haemodialysis: solute transfer, water removal and comparison
root.lessonIntent: Students distinguish solute diffusion from pressure-driven water removal in haemodialysis and compare mechanisms and source evidence with kidney function.
root.examSkill: State the modality and process, compare like with like, and qualify the evidence and model conditions.

voiceover.text: Renal Dialysis. Year eleven Biology. Cells to systems.

hook.heading: Two transport questions
hook.body: How does haemodialysis remove dissolved urea and excess water?
hook.callout: Solute diffusion and water ultrafiltration are distinct.
hook.caption: Haemodialysis replaces some kidney functions.

voiceover.text: Haemodialysis removes some wastes and excess water from blood when kidney function is inadequate. But these jobs do not rely on one mechanism. Urea transfer is mainly diffusive, while prescribed fluid removal uses pressure-driven ultrafiltration. We will compare these mechanisms with a working kidney. This lesson explains a model; it does not prescribe treatment or predict an individual's course.

concept-dialysis.heading: Solute transfer and fluid removal
concept-dialysis.body: A membrane separates blood from prescribed dialysate. Different driving forces move solutes and water.

bullets.text: Urea diffuses down its concentration gradient.
Dialysate composition affects net ion and glucose transfer.
Pressure-driven ultrafiltration removes excess water.
Cells and most large proteins are retained.

concept-dialysis.callout: The pictured particles illustrate solute diffusion only.
concept-dialysis.caption: Diffusion view only; pressure-driven fluid removal is a separate process.

voiceover.text: Blood and dialysate flow on opposite sides of a selectively permeable membrane. A urea concentration difference drives net diffusion into dialysate. The prescribed dialysate composition also affects ion and glucose exchange. Matching a concentration is a simplifying assumption for zero net diffusion of that solute, not a guarantee for all substances throughout treatment. Excess water is removed by a controlled pressure difference. The pictured diffusion model does not depict that water-removal mechanism.

concept-compare.body: Similar outcomes do not imply identical mechanisms or complete replacement.

bullets.text: Both help remove wastes and regulate fluid and solutes.
Kidney: filtration, reabsorption and secretion.
Haemodialysis: mainly diffusive solute transfer plus ultrafiltration.
Dialysis does not replace all renal endocrine functions.

concept-compare.callout: Compare a specified modality, not every treatment as one.
concept-compare.caption: Mechanism and function must both be compared.

voiceover.text: Both functioning kidneys and haemodialysis contribute to waste removal and water and solute balance. Kidneys combine filtration, reabsorption and secretion continuously. Haemodialysis transfers solutes mainly by diffusion and removes water by ultrafiltration; some solutes accompany the water by convection. Common schedules are intermittent, but regimens vary. Dialysis does not replace all endocrine functions of kidneys. A comparison should state what is represented and what is omitted.

bullets.text: Haemodialysis: blood treatment through an extracorporeal dialyser.
Dialysate: prescribed fluid across the exchange membrane.
Diffusion: net solute movement down a concentration gradient.
Ultrafiltration: pressure-driven fluid movement.
Convection: solutes carried with fluid flow.

definition.caption: Dialysis is broader than one machine-based modality.

voiceover.text: Haemodialysis uses a dialyser outside the body; renal dialysis also includes peritoneal methods that are outside this lesson's mechanism comparison. Dialysate is the treatment fluid on the opposite side of the exchange membrane. Diffusion is net solute movement down a concentration gradient. Ultrafiltration is fluid movement through a membrane driven by a pressure difference. Convection is solute carriage with that fluid flow.

concept-sources.body: Check evidence, methods, relevance, currency and potential conflicts for each claim.

bullets.text: What claim and patient or device context does it address?
Are the methods and evidence suitable?
Are sources independent, current and transparent about interests?

concept-sources.callout: A source category does not establish a universal reliability ranking.
concept-sources.caption: Evaluate the evidence behind each comparison.

voiceover.text: Evaluate the claim, not just the source label. An original study can support a measured result under defined conditions. A review can synthesise evidence, but methods, currency and conflicts still matter. A patient organisation may explain treatment clearly, while a manufacturer can supply device specifications that require independent checking. Agreement is stronger when sources are genuinely independent and use suitable evidence. Popularity or peer review alone is not a guarantee.

worked-example.question: Compare haemodialysis and a functioning kidney using two similarities and two differences. Identify the mechanism of water removal in haemodialysis.
worked-example.coachNote: Compare named mechanisms and functions; avoid claiming complete replacement.
steps: Both contribute to urea removal and fluid/solute balance.
Both normally retain blood cells behind a barrier.
Kidney: filtration, reabsorption and secretion; haemodialysis: mainly diffusion plus ultrafiltration.
The kidney regulates continuously and has endocrine roles; dialysis regimens vary and do not replace all roles.
In haemodialysis, excess water removal is pressure-driven ultrafiltration.
worked-example.caption: State similarities without erasing mechanistic differences.

voiceover.text: Write two similarities and two differences. Both kidney function and haemodialysis can remove urea and excess fluid, and both retain blood cells using a barrier. A kidney uses filtration and regulated tubular transport, whereas haemodialysis relies mainly on diffusive solute exchange plus pressure-driven water removal. Healthy kidneys regulate continuously and provide endocrine functions; haemodialysis regimens differ and do not replace all those functions. Neither identical glucose balance nor a universal schedule should be assumed.

misconception.heading: Two dialysis traps
misconception.body: Wrong: haemodialysis uses only diffusion and replaces every kidney function.
misconception.secondary: Urea transfer is mainly diffusive; fluid removal uses ultrafiltration. Regimens vary and endocrine functions are not fully replaced.
misconception.callout: A mechanism lesson is not a treatment recommendation.
misconception.caption: Dialysis provides partial replacement with modality-specific mechanisms.

voiceover.text: Haemodialysis does not use diffusion alone, and it does not restore every kidney function. Solute diffusion and pressure-driven ultrafiltration have different driving forces. Some dissolved solute is carried with fluid, too. Treatments and schedules are individualised. Decisions about dialysis and transplantation depend on clinical circumstances, so a school comparison should not turn into a universal treatment recommendation.

quick-check.question: A simple membrane model has urea higher in blood than fresh dialysate. What drives net urea diffusion? What separately drives excess-water removal in haemodialysis?
quick-check.pausePrompt: Pause: name the driving force for each process.
answerSteps: The urea concentration difference drives net diffusion towards dialysate.
A controlled transmembrane pressure difference drives ultrafiltration of water.
The two processes are distinct; some solute may also move by convection.
quick-check.caption: Identify the driving force for each transport process.

voiceover.text: Urea is higher in blood than fresh dialysate in a simple membrane model. What drives net urea diffusion, and what separately drives excess-water removal in haemodialysis? The urea concentration gradient drives net diffusion towards dialysate. A controlled pressure difference drives ultrafiltration of water. Some solutes can also be carried with the flowing water.

points: Urea transfer is mainly diffusive.
Excess water removal uses pressure-driven ultrafiltration.
Convection can accompany fluid flow.
Dialysate composition and treatment regimen matter.
Haemodialysis does not replace every kidney function.
summary.finalPrompt: Name the modality, transported substance and driving force.
summary.caption: Diffusion, ultrafiltration, partial replacement and evaluated evidence.

voiceover.text: Keep the mechanisms distinct. Urea crosses mainly by diffusion down a concentration gradient. Excess water is removed by pressure-driven ultrafiltration, which can carry some solute by convection. Dialysate composition matters, and a matched-solute model is not a universal guarantee. Haemodialysis replaces some kidney functions, with variable regimens and incomplete endocrine replacement. Support your comparison with evaluated sources.

response.promptText: Urea is higher in blood than fresh dialysate in a simple membrane model. What drives net urea diffusion, and what separately drives excess-water removal in haemodialysis?
response.answerText: The urea concentration gradient drives net diffusion towards dialysate. A controlled pressure difference drives ultrafiltration of water. Some solutes can also be carried with the flowing water.

root.subtitle: Water uptake, rate calculations and limits of inference
root.lessonIntent: Students calculate linear bubble rates and calibrated uptake volumes, evaluate repeatability and bias, and design a teacher-supervised transpiration investigation.
root.examSkill: Normalise time and capillary area before comparison. Separate measured uptake from inferred transpiration; do not assume equal or one-direction bias.

voiceover.text: Measuring Transpiration Rate. Year eleven Biology. Cells to systems.

hook.body: A bubble tracks water entering a shoot. Water leaving the leaves is a different measurement.
hook.callout: Storage changes can separate uptake from transpiration.
hook.caption: Uptake can be a useful proxy under stated conditions.

voiceover.text: A potometer tracks water uptake by a cut shoot, rather than directly collecting the vapour lost by leaves. Uptake and transpiration can differ while the shoot gains or loses stored water. Under stable conditions uptake can be a useful proxy, but an environmental change may create a lag. The bubble records a measurement, not an automatic explanation of every water movement.

concept-method.body: Record distance and time after acclimation and checks for leaks.

bullets.text: Use a teacher-approved procedure and risk assessment.
Cut under water and check seals to reduce air entry and leaks.
Linear bubble rate = distance ÷ time.
Volume uptake rate = capillary area × distance ÷ time.

concept-method.callout: mm/min is a linear rate; mm³/min is a volume rate.
concept-method.caption: 18 mm ÷ 6 min = 3 mm/min; volume requires capillary area.

voiceover.text: In a teacher-approved procedure, prepare the shoot under water and check seals to reduce air entry and leaks. After acclimation, record bubble distance and elapsed time. Eighteen millimetres in six minutes gives a linear bubble rate of three millimetres per minute. For a uniform calibrated capillary, multiply distance by its internal cross-sectional area to obtain volume. Distance per time alone is not a volume rate.

concept-fair-test.body: Control or monitor other variables, acclimation and treatment order.

bullets.text: Independent variable: specified air-speed treatment.
Dependent measure: bubble displacement per time, or calibrated volume per time.
Monitor temperature, light, humidity, leaf area and apparatus.
Greater uptake supports a transpiration inference only with justified assumptions.

concept-fair-test.callout: A difference in uptake is the measured result.
concept-fair-test.caption: Synthetic example: 3 mm/min versus 8 mm/min.

voiceover.text: Compare fan off with fan on using the same shoot and apparatus, while monitoring temperature, light and humidity. A fan can change more than air speed. Allow acclimation and consider treatment order and time drift. Here the linear rates are three and eight millimetres per minute. They show greater measured uptake in this example. Attributing that difference to transpiration requires the proxy assumptions and controls to hold.

concept-trust.body: Repeatability, validity and accuracy answer different questions.

bullets.text: Mean of 8.0, 7.6 and 8.4 mm/min = 8.0 mm/min.
Range = 8.4 − 7.6 = 0.8 mm/min.
Close repeats do not remove a common systematic error.
Storage, leaks and changing conditions can affect treatments differently.

concept-trust.callout: Do not infer accuracy from agreement alone.
concept-trust.caption: Synthetic repeats: mean 8.0 mm/min, range 0.8 mm/min.

voiceover.text: Repeated rates of eight, seven point six and eight point four millimetres per minute have a mean of eight and a range of zero point eight. Their agreement indicates repeatability under those conditions, not freedom from bias. A common leak could affect every run. Water storage can also change differently between treatments. Neither repeats nor normalising time proves that uptake equals transpiration or that errors cancel.

bullets.text: Potometer: apparatus used to estimate shoot water uptake.
Linear rate: bubble distance ÷ time.
Volume rate: internal capillary area × linear rate.
Transpiration: water-vapour loss from aerial surfaces.
Repeatability: agreement under specified repeat conditions.

definition.callout: A proxy needs assumptions and validation.
definition.caption: Keep the measured quantity and inferred process distinct.

voiceover.text: A potometer measures uptake through a calibrated water pathway. Its direct bubble measurement is distance over time; capillary area converts this to volume over time. Transpiration is water-vapour loss from aerial plant surfaces. A controlled variable is held sufficiently stable or accounted for, while repeatability describes agreement among repeated measurements under specified conditions. Accuracy concerns closeness to a suitable reference, and cannot be inferred from repeats alone.

worked-example.question: Synthetic data from the same uniform capillary: 18 mm in 6 min without a fan; 40 mm in 5 min with a fan. Its internal area is 0.50 mm². Calculate linear rates, volume rates and their ratio. State one inference limit.
worked-example.coachNote: Use rates, then multiply by the stated internal area. 1 mm³ = 1 μL.
steps: No fan: 18 ÷ 6 = 3 mm/min; fan: 40 ÷ 5 = 8 mm/min.
No fan volume: 0.50 × 3 = 1.5 mm³/min = 1.5 μL/min.
Fan volume: 0.50 × 8 = 4.0 mm³/min = 4.0 μL/min.
Greater measured uptake does not by itself prove equal transpiration or that only wind caused the difference.
worked-example.caption: Linear rates 3 and 8 mm/min; volume rates 1.5 and 4.0 μL/min.

voiceover.text: The same uniform capillary gives eighteen millimetres in six minutes without a fan, and forty millimetres in five minutes with it. The linear rates are three and eight millimetres per minute. Their ratio is eight divided by three, about two point seven. If the internal area is zero point five square millimetres, the volume rates are one point five and four cubic millimetres per minute. These synthetic results establish uptake differences, with causal interpretation still depending on controls and proxy assumptions.

misconception.body: Wrong: uptake must always slightly overstate transpiration, so the same error cancels.
misconception.secondary: Changing storage can make uptake higher or lower than simultaneous transpiration. Leaks and treatment changes can also create unequal bias.
misconception.callout: Use a water balance and evidence, not a stock limitation sentence.
misconception.caption: Uptake and loss can diverge in either direction during transients.

voiceover.text: It is tempting to say uptake always slightly overstates transpiration. That is not a general rule. If stored water is increasing, uptake can exceed water loss. If stored water is being depleted during a rapid response, transpiration can temporarily exceed uptake. Metabolism and apparatus errors also need consideration. Neither the sign nor the equality of the error across treatments is guaranteed by the potometer alone.

quick-check.question: In a simplified 5-minute water balance, a shoot takes up 20 μL and loses 26 μL by transpiration. Neglect metabolism and other fluxes. What happens to stored water, and which rate is larger?
quick-check.pausePrompt: Pause: change in storage = input − output.
answerSteps: Stored water decreased, so transpiration exceeded uptake in this interval.
quick-check.caption: A stated balance can disprove a universal bias direction.

voiceover.text: Over five minutes a shoot takes up twenty microlitres and loses twenty six by transpiration. Ignore other fluxes. What happens to stored water, and which rate is larger? Storage decreases by six microlitres. Uptake is four microlitres per minute and transpiration is five point two. Transpiration exceeded uptake during this interval.

points: A potometer estimates uptake, not vapour loss directly.
Linear rate = distance ÷ time.
Volume rate = internal capillary area × linear rate.
Repeatability does not prove accuracy or causal validity.
Storage changes and bias can affect the direction of the proxy error.
summary.finalPrompt: State what was measured, calculated and inferred.
summary.caption: Measure uptake, calculate with units, qualify transpiration inference.

voiceover.text: A potometer measures uptake, with bubble distance converted to a linear rate and capillary area used for a volume rate. Normalise unequal observation times and compare appropriate units. Repeat measurements, control relevant factors and check for systematic errors. Uptake is a conditional proxy for transpiration; changing storage can produce differences in either direction. A practical requires actual supervised measurements and records, not just viewing the synthetic example.

response.promptText: Over five minutes a shoot takes up twenty microlitres and loses twenty six by transpiration. Ignore other fluxes. What happens to stored water, and which rate is larger?
response.answerText: Storage decreases by six microlitres. Uptake is four microlitres per minute and transpiration is five point two. Transpiration exceeded uptake during this interval.

root.subtitle: Chromosome reduction and possible genetic combinations
root.inquiryQuestion: How does meiosis reduce chromosome number and generate genetic variation?
root.lessonIntent: Students model the named meiotic phases, distinguish possible combinations from products of one division, and explain why variation is not a uniqueness guarantee.
root.examSkill: Track homologues and chromatids, state assumptions for 2ⁿ, and distinguish meiotic processes from random fertilisation.

voiceover.text: Meiosis. Year eleven Biology. Cells as the basis of life.

hook.heading: Variation is not a guarantee
hook.body: Meiosis reduces chromosome number and can generate new combinations of existing alleles.
hook.callout: Many possible combinations does not mean no repeats.
hook.caption: Track chromosome number and allele combinations separately.

voiceover.text: Meiosis can generate extensive genetic variation while reducing chromosome number. That does not guarantee that every gamete is different from every other gamete. We will track chromosome number separately from allele combinations. A simple model can even produce repeated combinations among its four products. The useful question is how the mechanisms generate possibilities, not whether uniqueness is mathematically guaranteed.

concept-halving.heading: One replication, two divisions
concept-halving.body: A standard diploid meiosis yields four haploid nuclear products.

bullets.text: Before meiosis: one DNA replication.
Meiosis I separates homologous chromosomes.
Meiosis II separates sister chromatids, without another replication.
The model shows four haploid products, not four functional eggs.

concept-halving.callout: Chromosome number counts chromosomes, not DNA copies.
concept-halving.caption: Model: 2n = 4 becomes n = 2 after meiosis I and remains n = 2 after meiosis II.

voiceover.text: In the standard diploid model, DNA replicates once before meiosis. Homologues separate in meiosis one, leaving one member of each pair in each daughter nucleus. Sister chromatids separate in meiosis two without another DNA replication. The completed model produces four haploid nuclei. In sperm formation these can become four sperm, whereas human egg formation distributes cytoplasm unequally. In plants, meiosis produces spores rather than directly producing gametes. Our diagram represents chromosome reduction, not every life cycle.

concept-variation.body: Follow homologues, non-sister exchange and the resulting chromosome combinations.

bullets.text: Crossing over: corresponding segments exchanged between non-sister chromatids.
Independent orientation: each homologous pair can face either pole.
Segregation separates homologues in I and chromatids in II.
The illustrated allele outcomes depend on the starting genotype.

concept-variation.caption: One crossover example does not describe every meiotic outcome.

voiceover.text: During prophase one, crossing over can exchange corresponding DNA segments between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes. Homologous pairs orient independently at metaphase one, affecting which homologues segregate together. The resulting random segregation allocates homologues to daughter cells, followed by sister-chromatid separation in meiosis two. These descriptions are connected parts of the process; do not multiply assortment and segregation as if they were unrelated numerical bonuses. The illustrated crossover is one heterozygous example, not a guarantee that all products always differ.

concept-combined.heading: Possible combinations across many meioses
concept-combined.body: 2ⁿ counts whole-chromosome parental-origin combinations under stated assumptions.

bullets.text: n independently assorting pairs: 2ⁿ possible combinations.
3 pairs: 8 possibilities; 23 pairs: 8,388,608.
One meiosis has four nuclear products, not 2ⁿ products.
Random fertilisation adds offspring combinations after meiosis.

concept-combined.callout: Count possibilities separately from cells produced.
concept-combined.caption: The diagram enumerates possible types across many meiotic events.

voiceover.text: Ignoring crossing over, two to the power n counts possible whole-chromosome parental-origin combinations in a gamete across many meioses, for n independently assorting pairs. Three pairs give eight possibilities; twenty three give eight million, three hundred and eighty eight thousand, six hundred and eight. One meiosis does not produce that many cells. Nor are parental-origin labels necessarily distinct allele genotypes at every locus. Crossing over can add combinations where alleles differ. Random fertilisation is a later process combining gametes into offspring.

bullets.text: Homologues: chromosomes with corresponding loci, potentially different alleles.
Sister chromatids: copies of one chromosome, potentially altered by recombination.
Crossing over: exchange between non-sister chromatids in prophase I.
Independent assortment: independent orientation of homologous pairs.
Haploid: one member of each homologous pair.

definition.callout: Ploidy and genetic uniqueness are different properties.
definition.caption: Follow homologues, chromatids, alleles and ploidy.

voiceover.text: Homologous chromosomes carry corresponding loci, though their alleles can differ. Sister chromatids are the copied chromatids of one chromosome and may differ after recombination. Crossing over exchanges DNA between non-sister chromatids. Independent assortment describes the independent orientations of homologous pairs. Segregation is their subsequent separation, followed by chromatid separation in meiosis two. Haploid means one chromosome from each homologous pair, not that every haploid cell has a unique genotype.

worked-example.question: Using two distinguishable homologous pairs with duplicated chromatids and allele labels, construct and operate a phase-by-phase meiosis model. Repeat with a different orientation and record the products.
worked-example.coachNote: One pair cannot demonstrate independent orientation between different pairs.
steps: Prophase I: pair homologues; model one specified non-sister crossover.
Metaphase I: orient the two pairs independently.
Anaphase I, telophase I and cytokinesis: separate homologues into two cells.
Prophase II and metaphase II: prepare and align chromosomes without another replication.
Anaphase II, telophase II and cytokinesis: separate chromatids and record four haploid products.
Repeat an orientation; compare allele outcomes and assess model limits.
worked-example.caption: Actual construction, operation and a recorded comparison are required.

voiceover.text: Build two distinguishable homologous pairs, with duplicated chromatids and marked alleles. Model prophase one pairing and a specified non-sister crossover. Show independent pair orientation at metaphase one. Separate homologues at anaphase one, then represent telophase and cytokinesis. Without another replication, model prophase two, metaphase two, chromatid separation at anaphase two, and telophase two with cytokinesis. Record chromosome and allele outcomes, repeat with a different orientation, and explain what the pipe-cleaner model omits.

misconception.heading: Four products need not mean four types
misconception.body: Wrong: every meiosis guarantees four genetically different gametes.
misconception.secondary: In a one-pair model whose homologues differ only at A/a, with identical sister copies and no crossover or mutation, the four products are A, A, a and a: two model genotypes.
misconception.callout: A valid counterexample defeats a universal claim.
misconception.caption: A, A, a, a: four products, two allele types.

voiceover.text: Consider a simplified one-pair model in which the two homologues differ only at A and a. Sister copies are identical, and no crossing over or mutation occurs. After meiosis, two products carry A and two carry a, so the four products include repeated model genotypes. This counterexample rejects a universal uniqueness guarantee; it does not claim that normal human gametes have little diversity. Random fertilisation occurs after meiosis.

quick-check.question: A model has 2n = 6 with distinguishable parental-origin homologues and independent assortment, ignoring crossing over. How many whole-chromosome combinations are possible across many meioses? Does one meiosis produce that many cells?
quick-check.pausePrompt: Pause: calculate n, then separate possible types from products.
answerSteps: 2³ = 8 possible whole-chromosome combinations across many meioses.
One completed meiosis has four haploid nuclear products, not eight.
This count does not guarantee distinct allele genotypes at every locus.
quick-check.caption: Separate possible combinations from products of one meiosis.

voiceover.text: A model has a diploid number of six and independent assortment, ignoring crossing over. How many parental-origin whole-chromosome combinations are possible across many meioses? Does one meiosis produce that many cells? There are three homologous pairs, so two cubed gives eight possible combinations. One completed meiosis has four haploid nuclear products, not eight. Parental-origin combinations do not guarantee distinct allele genotypes at every locus.

points: One replication precedes two meiotic divisions.
Homologues separate in I; chromatids separate in II.
Recombination and assortment generate possibilities, not guaranteed uniqueness.
2ⁿ counts possible whole-chromosome combinations under stated assumptions.
Random fertilisation occurs after meiosis.
summary.finalPrompt: State which chromosomes, cells, alleles and assumptions you are counting.
summary.caption: Chromosome reduction, conditional variation and model evidence.

voiceover.text: One DNA replication is followed by two meiotic divisions. Homologues separate first and sister chromatids second, reducing chromosome number. Crossing over and independent orientation can generate allele combinations, but no universal uniqueness guarantee follows. Two to the power n counts possible parental-origin combinations under stated assumptions across many meioses. Random fertilisation then combines gametes. Demonstrate the phases with a model and retain your observations and evaluation.

response.answerText: There are three homologous pairs, so two cubed gives eight possible combinations. One completed meiosis has four haploid nuclear products, not eight. Parental-origin combinations do not guarantee distinct allele genotypes at every locus.
